extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity sleuths, and readers interested in retractions/misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: A news-category page aggregating reports of plagiarism and related research-misconduct incidents across journals, institutions, and countries; useful for spotting common indicators, procedural outcomes, and responses to alleged misconduct. The page compiles case descriptions and quotes from investigations, courts, and journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: implausible_sophistication_relative_to_authors
rubrics_metrics.description: The suspect work appears to be especially advanced to have been conducted by the listed authors (e.g., two high‑school students producing work unusually advanced for their level).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a red flag for potential misconduct when the technical sophistication, scope, or presumed resources required seem inconsistent with the authors’ background or available time (the page notes ViSEF projects must be completed in 12 months while students continue school).

rubrics_metrics.name: identical_or_near-identical_figures_or_graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphs or figures in the suspect work are almost identical to those in previously published research (sometimes plotted in a different color or thickness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even small cosmetic changes (color, thickness) do not negate the similarity; near‑identical figures suggest possible copying or unauthorized access to original raw data and are primary evidence for allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: completion_timeframe_and_eligibility_requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural eligibility constraints for competitions/publication (example: ViSEF projects must have been completed within a specified 12‑month period while authors continued school).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations or implausible adherence to such timeframes can indicate ineligible work or raise suspicion about when/where the work was produced; these rules are part of evaluating whether a submission legitimately represents the authors’ work.

rubrics_metrics.name: multiple_overlaps_with_published_work
rubrics_metrics.description: Detecting multiple overlaps between a submission (poster, manuscript) and previously published research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated overlapping passages, data, or figures across different parts of a submission strengthen a plagiarism case beyond a single coincidental similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: pattern_of_plagiarism_across_works
rubrics_metrics.description: A history or pattern of copying across multiple articles/books/grants (described in one case as 'massive' misconduct or a 'pattern of plagiarism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A systematic pattern (multiple books/articles) is treated more severely by funders/courts and can trigger sanctions such as repayment of grants, bans from applying for funding, and ordered retractions/withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: authorship_theft_or_identity_fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers published under someone else’s name where the listed author denies authorship (claims hacking/identity theft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorship fraud complicates provenance tracking; silent removals or lack of transparent notices can further obscure whether a paper ever legitimately existed. Investigations may need to determine how names were inserted or manipulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: paper_mill_activity_and_sold_authorship_slots
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that manuscripts were stolen and authorship slots were sold by a paper mill (e.g., offers on Telegram to buy authorship for low fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketplaces selling authorship or recycled/stolen manuscripts are indicators of organized misconduct; such activity explains how the same work can appear under different names and merited different journals' publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: near_verbatim_copying_with_minor_edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions that are near‑verbatim copies of another work, differing only by minor edits such as omitted footnotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Near‑verbatim reproduction (apart from trivial changes) is strong evidence of plagiarism, even when some footnotes or small elements are removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: identical_titles_images_and_metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Two works having identical titles, identical images/figures, and matching metadata across different authors or journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identical metadata and images are particularly damning because they are hard to explain by coincidence; journals and original authors often use these to prove copying and prompt retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: tortured_phrases_or_nonsensical_paraphrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of 'tortured phrases' — common terms transformed into nonsensical or awkward alternatives (example: 'broiler mortality' becoming 'grill mortality').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such unnatural substitutions are a hallmark of low‑quality paraphrasing or automated/malicious rewording used by paper mills and can flag plagiarized/repurposed content even when surface wording differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: citation_manipulation_and_citation_falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation stuffing or falsifying citations in conference proceedings or journals (referred to as 'citation falsification' and 'citation stuffing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulating citations undermines the scholarly record and has led organizations (e.g., ACM) to retract papers; detection of abnormal citation patterns is a criterion for misconduct investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: significant_unattributed_overlap_and_insufficient_data
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings of 'significant unattributed overlap' with another (published or unpublished) manuscript coupled with authors providing data that are 'insufficient to resolve the concerns.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When overlap is demonstrable and authors cannot substantiate provenance with adequate data, journals may retract the work; investigations may also uncover additional scientific errors during follow‑up.

rubrics_metrics.name: silent_removal_without_public_notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals silently remove a paper for plagiarism with no public retraction/correction notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of transparent correction notices raises questions about recordkeeping and accountability; it can hinder victims' ability to document and respond to plagiarism and complicate scholarly tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: legal_findings_and_sanctions_as_outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Court or funder decisions ordering repayment of grants, bans on funding applications, supervision restrictions, or court‑ordered retractions/withdrawals for proven plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and administrative sanctions (repayment, funding bans, ordered withdrawals) are concrete consequences used to enforce standards; their presence signals the severity and proof level reached in an investigation.
